messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Morales was thirty, married, and had spent the last decade working as a carpenter in and around Raleigh, moving from framing houses to finish work with the kind of steady physical competence he had always taken pride in. The traumatic event that still organized his days happened two years earlier on a summer afternoon at a jobsite, when a coworker’s hand was pulled into a saw and Daniel was the first to reach him. He remembered the suddenness of the blood, the raw tear of skin and bone, and the metallic, sugary taste of the coffee he had been drinking when he bent over the injured man. What stayed with him most was not a clear story he could tell from start to finish, but a flood of sensation that arrived all at once: the sight of the wound, the pressure of trying to hold the man still, the smell of wood dust and blood, and the taste in his mouth that seemed to belong to that moment forever.

In the months after, Daniel found that ordinary contact could jolt him back into that scene. A hand on his shoulder in a crowded aisle, a sudden grip from his wife when she was trying to get his attention, even the brief squeeze of a handshake at work could make his chest tighten. The same happened when he caught the taste of the coffee he had been drinking that day, or when he saw open cuts on another worker’s forearm after a minor accident on a site. Those moments would not just upset him; they would drag him immediately into the memory without warning, and he would feel as if he were standing over his coworker again, helpless and nauseated. When that happened, he would pull away from people, blank out on purpose, or eat far more than he wanted once he got home, using the heaviness of a meal to smother the feelings he could not otherwise control. Yet the eating never lasted as relief. He would finish feeling ashamed, and the shame only confirmed what he had already come to believe: that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that he had permanently changed for the worse, and that he could not rely on himself when anything unexpected happened.

That belief had also changed the way he made sense of the memory itself. Daniel was certain there was something wrong with him because the event never stayed in words; whenever he tried to describe it, the details collapsed, and what came back was not a narrative but a complete sensory reliving, vivid enough to feel the blood in his mouth and the weight of the injured hand all over again. He had come to believe that because he could not put it into words, he must be permanently damaged. The more he thought this, the more those sensations seemed to arrive on their own, triggered by the slightest reminder: a gloved hand brushing his arm, the coppery taste of a bitten lip, the sight of a fresh wound at the hardware store. Each reminder made him fear another wave of the same memory, and the fear itself made him watch for danger everywhere. At work he began scanning coworkers’ hands, forearms, and tools; at home he avoided talking about the incident with his wife because thinking about it even for a moment seemed to open the door to all of it.

Over time, his attempts to manage the distress only deepened his sense that he was failing. He would deliberately try to leave his body, sitting in the truck after work and staring through himself, or he would eat until he felt numb, telling himself that at least then he was not thinking about the event. But each time he used those strategies, he woke up feeling more disconnected and more convinced that something essential in him had been altered. That conviction made the world feel more dangerous and the reminders more potent. He became more alert to touch, to the taste of coffee, to any visible injury, and because he was watching so closely, he noticed them everywhere. In a carpentry job, where hands are always in motion and minor cuts are common, he found it hard to stay present when a coworker reached for a tool or when someone walked in from a site with a scraped knuckle. At home his wife noticed he flinched when she touched him from behind, and he withdrew from the easy physical closeness that had once been natural in their marriage.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by the cycle and frightened by how quickly it could seize him. He was not simply haunted by one memory; he was living around it, shaping his days to avoid thinking, bracing for touch, scanning for injuries, and then hating himself for how easily he was pulled back under. What finally brought him in was a stretch of evenings in which he found himself eating in secret after work, blanking out in the truck, and then sitting at the kitchen table unable to explain to his wife why he felt so broken. He came hoping to regain some trust in himself and to stop feeling as though one summer afternoon had permanently taken his life away.
